description: Major muscles, agonist and antagonist roles, and isotonic and isometric contractions in sporting actions.
content_html:
Why Muscles Work in Pairs

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. Because of this, every joint in the body is controlled by at least two muscles that work in opposite directions. When one muscle contracts and shortens to produce movement, the opposing muscle relaxes and lengthens to allow that movement. This arrangement is called an antagonistic muscle pair. Understanding these pairs — and always naming them in the context of a specific joint and a specific direction of movement — is essential for exam answers.

Major Muscles of the Body

At the shoulder, the deltoid forms the rounded cap of the shoulder. It is the prime mover for abduction of the arm (lifting it out to the side) and also contributes to flexion and extension. The rotator cuffs are a group of four muscles that wrap around the shoulder joint, stabilising the ball-and-socket joint and assisting rotation — critical in throwing sports such as cricket bowling and javelin. The pectorals (chest muscles) lie across the front of the thorax and act as prime movers in horizontal adduction, such as in the push-up or front crawl pull phase. The latissimus dorsi (‘lats’) is the large fan-shaped muscle of the back, responsible for extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder, powerful in swimming and rowing movements.

At the elbow, the biceps sits on the front of the upper arm. During elbow flexion (the upward phase of a bicep curl), the biceps is the agonist (prime mover), contracting concentrically to shorten and pull the forearm up. On the back of the upper arm sits the triceps. During elbow flexion, the triceps acts as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow movement. The roles reverse completely during elbow extension (the downward phase of a press-up): the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps becomes the antagonist.

At the hip and knee, two large muscle groups dominate. The quadriceps group (four muscles on the front of the thigh) is the prime mover for knee extension — straightening the knee. The hamstrings lie on the back of the thigh and are the prime mover for knee flexion (bending the knee). At the knee, the quadriceps and hamstrings form the classic antagonistic pair: quadriceps agonist during extension, hamstrings agonist during flexion. The gluteals are the large buttock muscles that drive hip extension — critical in sprinting and jumping. The hip flexors are the antagonists to the gluteals, acting as agonists during hip flexion (lifting the knee forwards in running).

At the ankle, the gastrocnemius runs from behind the knee down to the heel via the Achilles tendon. It is the prime mover for plantar flexion — pointing the toes down, as in sprinting push-off or jumping. The tibialis anterior on the front of the lower leg is the prime mover for dorsiflexion (pulling the toes upward), and the two muscles form an antagonistic pair at the ankle.

The abdominals are the core muscles on the front of the trunk. They flex the spine, stabilise the pelvis during running and throwing, and are active in almost every sporting movement as a postural stabiliser.

Key Fact

In a bicep curl upward phase: biceps = agonist (concentric contraction), triceps = antagonist. In kicking (knee extension): quadriceps = agonist, hamstrings = antagonist. In a sprinting push-off (plantar flexion): gastrocnemius = agonist, tibialis anterior = antagonist.

A very common error in exams is to name a single muscle as ‘the agonist’ without specifying the joint, the direction of movement, or the antagonist. Mark schemes award marks for the complete picture: agonist named (1), antagonist named (1), action described at the correct joint (1). Writing ‘the biceps is the agonist’ alone will not earn full marks. Always frame answers as: “During elbow flexion, the biceps acts as the agonist (prime mover) while the triceps acts as the antagonist at the elbow joint.”

Types of Muscle Contraction

Muscles do not always contract in the same way. The spec identifies three types of contraction: isotonic concentric, isotonic eccentric and isometric.

Isotonic concentric contraction occurs when a muscle shortens while it contracts, producing movement. The biceps during the upward phase of a bicep curl contracts concentrically — it shortens, and the elbow flexes. This is the most obvious form of contraction in sport: the quadriceps contracts concentrically to extend the knee when kicking a ball.

Isotonic eccentric contraction occurs when a muscle produces tension while it lengthens. This happens when the muscle is acting as a brake. During the downward phase of a bicep curl, the biceps contracts eccentrically — it is still producing tension to control the lowering of the weight, but it is getting longer as the elbow extends. Eccentric contractions are responsible for DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) because the lengthening under load causes tiny tears in muscle fibres.

Isometric contraction occurs when a muscle is active but the joint does not move. A gymnast holding a crucifix position on the rings keeps the arms outstretched perfectly still — the deltoids and pectorals are working hard isometrically. A rugby player locked in a scrum uses isometric contractions to maintain position against an opposing force.

Key Fact

Concentric = muscle shortens (produces movement). Eccentric = muscle lengthens under tension (controls or brakes movement). Isometric = muscle produces tension but no joint movement occurs. All three can happen in the same exercise: a squat involves concentric quadriceps on the way up, eccentric on the way down, and isometric if you pause at the bottom.

Tendons are strong, inelastic connective tissues that attach muscles to bones. Without tendons, a muscle contraction would not move the skeleton. The Achilles tendon, for example, attaches the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles to the calcaneus (heel bone). When the calf muscles contract concentrically, the Achilles tendon transmits the force to the heel, producing plantar flexion for sprinting. Tendons are denser and less elastic than muscles, which is why they take longer to strengthen with training. Overloading tendons without adequate rest is a common cause of injury in growing athletes.
exam_tip_html: For any question asking about agonist and antagonist muscles, always include three elements: (1) the name of the agonist (prime mover), (2) the name of the antagonist, and (3) the specific joint and direction of movement. Missing any of these costs marks. On a 4-mark ‘Explain’ question, the mark scheme typically awards 1 mark for each element plus 1 for an accurate description of the type of contraction (concentric or eccentric). For contraction-type questions, the trick is to ask yourself: ‘Is the muscle getting shorter (concentric) or longer (eccentric) while it is working?’ A common error is to say the antagonist ‘contracts’ — the antagonist actually relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement to occur.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Muscles work in antagonistic pairs: the agonist (prime mover) contracts to produce movement at a joint while the antagonist relaxes and lengthens. Always name both muscles and the joint when answering exam questions.
  • Concentric contraction = muscle shortens (producing movement); eccentric contraction = muscle lengthens under tension (controlling or braking movement); isometric contraction = muscle produces tension with no change in length and no joint movement.
  • Key sporting pairs: biceps/triceps at the elbow, quadriceps/hamstrings at the knee, gastrocnemius/tibialis anterior at the ankle, deltoid acting with the lats at the shoulder. Tendons connect each muscle to its bone attachment point.

practice_questions.text: During a pull-up exercise, a gymnast bends her elbows to raise her body upward. Name the agonist muscle acting at the elbow joint during this upward phase.
Define the term 'isometric contraction' and give one sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for definition: a contraction where the muscle produces tension but does not change length and no joint movement occurs; 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. gymnast holding a crucifix on the rings / rugby player in a scrum / holding a plank position).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to the quadriceps and hamstrings during the upward phase of a squat (knee extension from a bent position to standing).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the quadriceps as the agonist during knee extension; 1 mark for stating the quadriceps contracts concentrically (shortens under tension) to produce knee extension; 1 mark for stating the hamstrings act as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow the movement to occur.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between concentric and eccentric contraction, using the biceps muscle as an example in both cases.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining concentric contraction: the biceps shortens under tension during elbow flexion (upward phase of bicep curl); 1 mark for explaining eccentric contraction: the biceps lengthens under tension during elbow extension (lowering phase of bicep curl) to control the movement; 1 mark for correctly linking concentric to movement production; 1 mark for correctly linking eccentric to movement control or braking (and noting this is why DOMS can occur).

practice_questions.text: A club-level badminton player notices that her forehand smash relies on coordinated muscle action at the shoulder and elbow. Analyse the role of antagonistic muscle pairs in producing this movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear identification of at least two antagonistic pairs relevant to the movement (e.g. deltoid/latissimus dorsi at the shoulder; triceps/biceps at the elbow); each pair discussed in terms of agonist and antagonist roles with correct contraction types (concentric/eccentric) applied to specific phases of the smash; consistent sporting application throughout; technically accurate language throughout.

Secure: Two pairs identified; mostly correct agonist/antagonist assignment; contraction types mentioned but may not be consistently linked to specific phases; generally applied to the smash.

Developing: One pair discussed with development; or two pairs identified but with limited contraction type analysis; sporting context present but superficial.

Emerging: Basic mention of agonist/antagonist with little development; incorrect assignment possible; limited sporting application.

Acceptable content: at the shoulder, the deltoid (agonist) contracts concentrically during abduction/flexion to raise the arm; the latissimus dorsi (antagonist) relaxes; at the elbow, the triceps (agonist) contracts concentrically during extension to produce the smashing action; the biceps (antagonist) relaxes and lengthens; on the follow-through, the roles reverse as the biceps contracts eccentrically to decelerate the arm.

practice_questions.text: A sprint coach claims that eccentric muscle contractions are just as important as concentric contractions for athletic performance. Evaluate this claim, referring to specific muscles and sporting actions in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of both concentric and eccentric contractions; multiple sporting examples applied accurately; candidate demonstrates understanding of eccentric loading (DOMS, injury risk, deceleration, landing mechanics) alongside the more obvious role of concentric power production; balanced argument with a justified conclusion.

Secure: Both types discussed with relevant examples; most points accurate; conclusion present; some sporting application.

Developing: One type discussed more fully than the other; limited sporting examples; argument is one-sided.

Emerging: Basic description of contractions with little evaluation or sporting application.

Agreeing (eccentric is equally important): eccentric contractions of the hamstrings decelerate the leg after a kick, preventing knee injury; the biceps contracts eccentrically to control the lowering phase of a pull-up, building strength through a full range; the quadriceps contracts eccentrically during landing from a jump to absorb force and protect the knee; eccentric loading in plyometric training (depth jumps) maximises the stretch-shortening cycle for explosive power.

Disagreeing / partial challenge: concentric power is what drives the explosive movements in sprinting, jumping and throwing; most spectators and coaches focus on concentric strength as it directly produces performance outcomes; without concentric quadriceps power, there would be no sprint speed to decelerate.

knowledge_checks.q: Which muscle is the agonist during elbow flexion in a bicep curl upward phase?
What type of contraction occurs when a muscle lengthens under tension to control movement?
During knee extension (kicking), the _____ is the agonist while the hamstrings act as the antagonist.
The _____ muscle on the back of the upper arm acts as the agonist during elbow extension.
Match each muscle to its primary action:
right: Abduction of the arm at the shoulder

flashcard_questions.q: What is an antagonistic muscle pair?
flashcard_questions.a: Two muscles working in opposite directions: one contracts while the other relaxes.

flashcard_questions.q: During elbow flexion, the biceps is the agonist. What is the antagonist?
flashcard_questions.a: Triceps — it relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a concentric muscle contraction?
flashcard_questions.a: The muscle shortens under tension, producing joint movement.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an eccentric muscle contraction?
flashcard_questions.a: The muscle lengthens under tension to control or brake movement.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of contraction does a gymnast use to hold a static crucifix position?
flashcard_questions.a: Isometric — tension produced but no joint movement occurs.

flashcard_questions.q: Which muscle is the prime mover for plantar flexion at the ankle?
Which muscle group is the agonist for knee extension?
The deltoid caps the shoulder. What is its prime movement?
flashcard_questions.a: Abduction of the arm (lifting the arm out to the side).

flashcard_questions.q: What causes DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness)?
flashcard_questions.a: Eccentric contractions causing tiny tears in muscle fibres.
Attach muscles to bones, transmitting contractile force to produce movement.

flashcard_questions.q: Which muscle on the back of the thigh is the agonist during knee flexion?
During the downward phase of a bicep curl, what type of contraction does the biceps perform?
flashcard_questions.a: Eccentric — it lengthens under tension to control the lowering.

flashcard_questions.q: The latissimus dorsi is the large back muscle. What movement does it produce at the shoulder?
flashcard_questions.a: Extension and adduction of the arm.

glossary_terms.definition: A pair of muscles that work in opposite directions across a joint: when the agonist contracts, the antagonist relaxes, and vice versa.
The triangular muscle capping the shoulder joint, responsible for abduction of the arm.
The muscle on the front of the upper arm that acts as the prime mover for elbow flexion.
The muscle on the back of the upper arm that acts as the prime mover for elbow extension.
A group of muscles on the back of the thigh that acts as the prime mover for knee flexion and assists hip extension.
The large muscle of the calf, acting as the prime mover for plantar flexion (pointing the foot downwards).
A type of muscle contraction where the muscle shortens under tension as it produces movement.
A type of muscle contraction where the muscle lengthens under tension while controlling movement.
A type of muscle contraction where the muscle produces tension but does not change length and no joint movement occurs.
